alternatives.why: Same interpreter on a trimmed Debian: no compilers, docs or locales, so far less to scan and to patch.
Smallest of the official tags, but musl instead of glibc — wheels often have to be built from source.
No shell and no package manager: much smaller attack surface, and much harder to debug inside.
Same runtime without the build toolchain that ships in the default tag.
Smallest official tag; native modules may need rebuilding against musl.
Runtime only — no shell, no npm — for an app whose dependencies are already installed at build time.
Drops the documentation and build packages from the default tag.
Smallest official tag; native gems need musl-compatible builds.
openjdk is deprecated on Docker Hub; Temurin is the maintained successor, and a JRE tag omits the compiler a running service does not need.
Same runtime on a much smaller base.
A running service needs the runtime, not the compiler.
No shell and no package manager around the JVM.
A statically linked Go binary needs no distribution at all. Build in golang, ship the binary here.
For binaries that still need libc or CA certificates.
Keeps a shell for debugging while staying small; needs CGO disabled or a musl build.
Ships the compiled binary and libgcc, without the 1 GB toolchain used to produce it.
A familiar base for a binary that needs a shell nearby.
FPM rather than the bundled Apache, on a smaller base.
For workers and console commands, which do not need a web server at all.
Roughly a fifth of the size, same configuration.
Runs as a non-root user and listens on 8080, so no privileged port and no root process.
Same server, much smaller base.
A different server: automatic HTTPS and a smaller configuration surface, if the Apache-specific config is not needed.
Same server, a fraction of the packages.
Same server on a smaller base.
Smaller, but note the locale and collation differences from the Debian tags — an existing data directory may not be readable across the two.
The slim tag drops tooling the server does not need at run time.
A drop-in-compatible server for most workloads, with a different maintenance cadence.
Built on a Red Hat universal base image, which some environments prefer for support reasons.
Pin the minor version rather than tracking the major tag: MongoDB's storage format changes between them.
Smaller base; the management plugin has its own tag suffix.
A smaller general-purpose base with the same package tooling.
Much smaller, but musl and BusyBox differ from glibc and GNU tools in ways that surface at run time.
Same distribution without the extras the default tag carries.
For an image that only needs to run one compiled binary.
Pin the minor version. `alpine:latest` moves between major releases, which changes musl and the package set under you.
If the shell is only there for the entrypoint, removing it removes the most useful thing an attacker finds inside.
Pin the minor version: Traefik's configuration format has changed between majors.
Already small; pin the version rather than following the rolling tag.
Same proxy on a smaller base.
The vendor's own registry is the one that receives security updates first.
FPM behind your own web server, on a smaller base.
